title: Advanced FastAPI and Production Deployment
subtitle: Make FastAPI services production-ready: OAuth2 and JWT authentication with hashed passwords, SQLAlchemy and Alembic, background work, thorough tests, and Docker images served by Uvicorn workers behind Nginx.
outcomes: Secure an API with the OAuth2 password flow, Argon2-hashed passwords and short-lived JWT access tokens
Persist data with SQLAlchemy 2.0 and a session per request, and change the schema safely with Alembic migrations
Move slow work off the request path with background tasks and task queues, without blocking the event loop
Test endpoints, authentication, ownership and background work with TestClient, dependency overrides and isolated databases
Package the service in a Docker image configured by environment variables, with structured logs and health checks
Run it with Uvicorn or Gunicorn workers behind Nginx, with the forwarded headers and root path it needs
prerequisites: Introduction to FastAPI and Modern Web Services, or the same experience: routers, Pydantic models and dependencies. Comfort with pytest (CI/CD and Automated Testing covers it) and basic SQL. You need Python 3.11 or later, a terminal with curl, and Docker with Docker Compose for the last lab; Containerisation and Orchestration with Docker and Kubernetes is useful background but not required.
description:
Getting a FastAPI app to answer on localhost is the easy part. This course covers what it takes to run one for real users. You'll secure it with the OAuth2 password flow, passwords stored only as Argon2 hashes and expiring JSON Web Tokens, with dependencies that keep each user's data their own; persist it with SQLAlchemy 2.0 and evolve the schema with Alembic migrations; keep responses fast with background tasks and know when a task queue such as Celery is the better tool; and test the whole service against isolated databases with dependency overrides. Then you'll make it production-shaped: configuration and secrets from the environment, JSON logs with request IDs, liveness and readiness checks, a non-root Docker image, Uvicorn or Gunicorn workers, and Nginx in front with the forwarded headers set up correctly.

The labs build one service, TaskHub, step by step, with starter files, TODOs and the real output of every command, from alembic upgrade to a request logged through the proxy, checked against current FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.1, PyJWT and pwdlib. The capstone takes your own task API all the way to a secure, tested, containerised deployment.

modules.title: Security and Authentication (JWT/OAuth2)
modules.summary: Secure an API the way FastAPI's security tools are designed for: the OAuth2 password flow with bearer tokens, passwords stored only as Argon2 hashes, signed JSON Web Tokens that expire, and dependencies that check who the caller is and what they may do.

lessons.title: OAuth2, tokens and the password flow
objectives: Explain how OAuth2 bearer tokens protect an API
Describe the password flow, where it fits and where it doesn't
Tell authentication from authorisation, and 401 from 403
key_points: OAuth2 is an authorisation framework: a client gets an access token from a token endpoint and sends it with every request as Authorization: Bearer <token>; the API checks the token, not a password, on each call.

In the password flow the client posts the username and password as form fields to the token URL and gets an access token back. It suits a first-party client you trust; OAuth security guidance (RFC 9700) advises against it in general, so third-party apps and single sign-on use the authorization code flow with PKCE.

fastapi.security.OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token") is a dependency that reads the bearer token from the Authorization header and answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer when it's missing; OAuth2PasswordRequestForm reads the login form, which needs python-multipart.
Authentication says who the caller is; authorisation decides what they may do. Answer 401 Unauthorized for missing or invalid credentials, and 403 Forbidden for a known caller who isn't allowed.
Swagger UI's Authorize button follows the tokenUrl: it posts the username and password, keeps the token and sends it with every request you try.

lessons.title: Hashing passwords
objectives: Store passwords safely with a password-hashing algorithm
Verify logins without revealing which usernames exist
key_points: Never store passwords, even encrypted: store a slow, salted hash from a password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt, never a fast general-purpose hash such as SHA-256 or MD5.

pwdlib (pip install "pwdlib[argon2]") is what FastAPI's documentation uses: PasswordHash.recommended() hashes with Argon2id, hash() returns one string holding the algorithm, its parameters, a random salt and the hash, and verify(password, hashed) checks a login.
Every hash has its own random salt, so the same password hashed twice gives two different strings: always compare with verify(), never by hashing again and comparing the strings.
Make an unknown username take as long as a wrong password, by verifying against a dummy hash, and give both the same error message, so attackers can't find out which accounts exist.

Passlib, used in many older tutorials, hasn't had a release since 2020. pwdlib's verify_and_update(password, hashed) also returns a new hash when the stored one uses outdated settings, so hashes can be upgraded at login.

lessons.title: JSON Web Tokens
objectives: Read the parts of a JWT and say what its signature proves
Create and verify expiring tokens with PyJWT
key_points: A JWT is three base64url parts separated by dots: a header naming the algorithm, a payload of claims, such as sub (the subject), iat (issued at) and exp (expiry), and a signature. Anyone can read the payload, so never put secrets in it.

The signature proves the token was issued by whoever holds the key and hasn't been changed. HS256 uses one shared secret, fine when one service issues and checks tokens; RS256 and ES256 sign with a private key and verify with a public one, for separate services.

With PyJWT, jwt.encode({"sub": "ana", "exp": expires}, key, algorithm="HS256") makes a token, and jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["HS256"]) checks its signature and expiry, raising ExpiredSignatureError or another InvalidTokenError. Always pass the list of allowed algorithms.
Keep access tokens short-lived, minutes rather than days, and the key out of the code: make one with python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))" and load it from the environment.
JWTs are stateless: the API doesn't store them, so it can't revoke one before it expires without extra machinery, such as a deny-list, or very short access tokens with refresh tokens.

walkthrough.title: Make, read and break a JWT

steps.do: With PyJWT installed (pip install pyjwt), start python3 and make a token that expires in 15 minutes.
steps.code:
import secrets
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

import jwt

key = secrets.token_hex(32)
token = jwt.encode({"sub": "ana", "exp": datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(minutes=15)}, key, algorithm="HS256")
token.count("."), jwt.get_unverified_header(token)
steps.see: (2, {'alg': 'HS256', 'typ': 'JWT'}): three parts, and a header anyone can read.

steps.do: Read the claims without the key: the payload is only encoded, not encrypted.
steps.code: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})

steps.do: Verify it properly, then with the wrong key.
steps.code:
jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["HS256"])["sub"]
jwt.decode(token, secrets.token_hex(32), algorithms=["HS256"])
steps.see: 'ana', then InvalidSignatureError: Signature verification failed

steps.do: An expired token is refused, and so is a decode that doesn't say which algorithms are allowed.
steps.code:
old = jwt.encode({"sub": "ana", "exp": datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(seconds=1)}, key, algorithm="HS256")
jwt.decode(old, key, algorithms=["HS256"])
jwt.decode(token, key)
steps.see: ExpiredSignatureError: Signature has expired, then DecodeError: It is required that you pass in a value for the "algorithms" argument when calling decode(). All three errors are InvalidTokenError subclasses, so one except clause handles them.

lessons.title: Protecting routes: current user, roles and scopes
objectives: Protect routes with a current-user dependency and role checks
Know what scopes and CORS add, and what they don't
key_points: get_current_user(token = Depends(oauth2_scheme)) decodes the token, loads the user and raises 401 if anything fails; an endpoint then asks for user: Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_user)].
Chained dependencies add rules: get_active_user depends on get_current_user and rejects disabled accounts with 403, and require_admin depends on get_active_user and checks the role.
OAuth2 scopes let a token carry finer permissions, such as tasks:write: declare them with Security(get_current_user, scopes=[...]) and check them in the dependency through SecurityScopes.
Hide other users' data completely: answer 404, not 403, for someone else's task, so IDs reveal nothing about what exists.

Serve tokens only over HTTPS and never log Authorization headers. CORS (CORSMiddleware with explicit allow_origins) controls which websites may call the API from browser JavaScript; it isn't authentication.

modules.title: Database Integration (SQLAlchemy)
modules.summary: Persist data properly: SQLAlchemy 2.0's typed models, one session per request through a dependency, ownership enforced in queries, schema changes managed with Alembic migrations, and when async database access is worth it.

lessons.title: SQLAlchemy 2.0: engines, models and sessions
objectives: Define typed ORM models in SQLAlchemy 2.0 style
Create, query and change rows with a Session
key_points: SQLAlchemy has two layers: Core, for SQL expressions and connections, and the ORM, which maps classes to tables. Version 2.0 brought the typed style used here: DeclarativeBase, Mapped[...] and mapped_column().

create_engine("sqlite:///./taskhub.db") makes an engine, a pool of connections to one database. The URL chooses the database and driver, so moving to PostgreSQL (postgresql+psycopg://...) changes the URL, not the models.

A model is a class with __tablename__ and typed columns: id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True), title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200)), and due: Mapped[date | None] for a nullable column; relationship() links models.

A Session tracks objects and turns changes into SQL inside a transaction: session.add(task), then session.commit(); session.get(Task, 1) loads by primary key, and session.scalars(select(Task).where(Task.owner_id == 1)).all() runs a query.
Base.metadata.create_all(engine) creates missing tables, which is handy for tests and demos, but it never changes tables that exist: use migrations for that.

lessons.title: Sessions as dependencies, and layers
objectives: Give each request its own session through a dependency
Keep ORM models and API schemas apart, and handle database errors
key_points: Give each request its own session from a yield dependency: def get_session(): with SessionLocal() as session: yield session. The with block closes it even when the endpoint fails.
Within one request, every dependency that asks for the session gets the same one, so a lookup dependency and the endpoint share it and their changes are committed together.
FastAPI runs def endpoints in a thread pool, so a SQLite engine needs connect_args={"check_same_thread": False}; each request still uses a session of its own.
Keep ORM models (the tables) and Pydantic schemas (the API's contract) separate; model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True) lets a response model read an ORM object's attributes.

Commit once per unit of work and roll back on errors, such as an IntegrityError from a unique constraint, answered with 409. Avoid N+1 queries: selectinload(User.tasks) loads a list's relationships in one extra query.

lessons.title: Migrations with Alembic
objectives: Set up Alembic and generate migrations from the models
Apply, revert and deploy schema changes safely
key_points: Alembic versions the database schema: each migration is a Python file with upgrade() and downgrade(), applied in order and recorded in the alembic_version table.

alembic init migrations creates alembic.ini and a migrations folder. In migrations/env.py, set the URL from your settings and target_metadata = Base.metadata, after importing the models, so autogenerate can compare the models with the database.

alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add archived flag" writes a migration from the differences. Read it before applying it: autogenerate can't see everything, and a renamed column comes out as a drop and an add.
alembic upgrade head applies pending migrations, alembic downgrade -1 reverts the last one, and alembic current and alembic history show where a database stands.
A new NOT NULL column needs a server_default, so existing rows get a value; SQLite can't alter tables freely, so set render_as_batch=True and Alembic recreates the table when it has to.
Run migrations as a deployment step before the new code takes traffic, and keep them backward compatible: add first and remove in a later release, so old and new versions can run side by side.

lessons.title: Async database access
objectives: Use SQLAlchemy's asyncio extension with an async driver
Decide when async database access is worth it
key_points: SQLAlchemy's asyncio extension provides create_async_engine and AsyncSession, used with await: result = await session.scalars(select(Task)).

It needs an async driver, aiosqlite for SQLite (sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db) or asyncpg or psycopg for PostgreSQL, and, from SQLAlchemy 2.1, the asyncio extra for greenlet: pip install "sqlalchemy[asyncio]".
async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False) makes sessions; without expire_on_commit=False, reading an attribute after a commit would need a new query, which async code can't run implicitly.
Lazy loading doesn't happen implicitly under asyncio (it raises MissingGreenlet): load relationships eagerly with selectinload(), or await obj.awaitable_attrs.tasks.
Async database access pays off when many requests wait on the database at once; a synchronous session in def endpoints, run in the thread pool, is simpler and serves many applications well.

steps.do: In a virtual environment, install SQLAlchemy with its asyncio extra and the async SQLite driver.
steps.code: pip install "sqlalchemy[asyncio]" aiosqlite

steps.do: Create async_demo.py.
steps.code:
import asyncio

from sqlalchemy import String, select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Task(Base):
    __tablename__ = "tasks"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))


engine = create_async_engine("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./async-demo.db")
SessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)


async def get_session():
    async with SessionLocal() as session:
        yield session


async def main():
    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        await conn.run_sync(Base.metadata.drop_all)
        await conn.run_sync(Base.metadata.create_all)
    async with SessionLocal() as session:
        session.add_all([Task(title="Write the release notes"), Task(title="Fix the login bug")])
        await session.commit()
        tasks = (await session.scalars(select(Task).order_by(Task.id))).all()
        print([t.title for t in tasks])
    await engine.dispose()


asyncio.run(main())

"""TaskHub: a production-ready task API."""

from functools import lru_cache

from pydantic import SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Settings from environment variables named TASKHUB_..., or from a .env file in development."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="TASKHUB_", env_file=".env")

    secret_key: SecretStr  # required: there is deliberately no default
    database_url: str = "sqlite:///./taskhub.db"
    access_token_minutes: int = 15
    outbox_path: Path = Path("outbox.jsonl")
    log_level: str = "INFO"
    log_json: bool = False


@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    """Read the settings once; tests can override this dependency."""
    return Settings()

def make_engine(url: str):

def create_access_token(subject: str, minutes: int | None = None) -> str:
    settings = get_settings()

    payload = {"sub": subject, "iat": now, "exp": expires}
    return jwt.encode(payload, settings.secret_key.get_secret_value(), algorithm=ALGORITHM)


def authenticate(session: Session, username: str, password: str) -> User | None:
    user = session.scalar(select(User).where(User.username == username))
    if user is None:

        return None
    return user if password_hash.verify(password, user.hashed_password) else None

    except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
        raise CREDENTIALS_ERROR from None
    user = session.scalar(select(User).where(User.username == claims.get("sub")))
    if user is None:

    return user

modules.title: Asynchronous Operations & Background Tasks
modules.summary: Keep responses fast without losing work: what really blocks the event loop and how to avoid it, lifespan set-up and shutdown, BackgroundTasks for short jobs after the response, and task queues such as Celery for work that must survive restarts.

lessons.title: The event loop, blocking code and lifespan
objectives: Keep blocking and CPU-heavy work off the event loop
Set up and clean up shared resources with a lifespan function
key_points: Blocking code inside async def stalls every request on that worker. Run it in the thread pool with await run_in_threadpool(func, *args) from fastapi.concurrency or await asyncio.to_thread(func, *args), or make the endpoint a plain def.
Call other services with an async client and reuse it: one httpx.AsyncClient for the application's lifetime keeps a pool of connections. Set a timeout on every call.
asyncio.gather runs independent awaits concurrently, and asyncio.timeout(seconds), from Python 3.11, bounds a group of them; return_exceptions=True stops one failure from cancelling the rest.
CPU-bound work, such as image processing or model inference, gains nothing from async: run it in more worker processes, a ProcessPoolExecutor or a task queue.

A lifespan function, @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app): ...; yield; ..., passed as FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan), runs set-up before the first request and clean-up at shutdown, replacing the older on_event handlers.

lessons.title: BackgroundTasks
objectives: Run short jobs after the response with BackgroundTasks
Know the limits of in-process background work
key_points: BackgroundTasks runs a function after the response has been sent: add a background: BackgroundTasks parameter, call background.add_task(send_email, user.email, subject), and the client doesn't wait.
Background tasks run in the same process, in the order they were added: def functions in the thread pool and async def functions on the event loop. Dependencies can add tasks too.
They suit short, best-effort work, such as sending an email or a webhook, writing an audit record or warming a cache.
Give a background job its own database session, because the request's session is closed by the time it runs: pass IDs and a session factory, not ORM objects.

Tasks are lost if the process stops or crashes, have no retries or results, and their failures never reach the client, so log them. With TestClient, background tasks finish before the call returns, so tests can check their effects at once.

lessons.title: Task queues: Celery and friends
objectives: Explain how a task queue moves work out of the API process
Choose between BackgroundTasks and a queue
key_points: A task queue moves work to separate worker processes through a message broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ: the API enqueues a job and answers at once, usually 202 Accepted with a job ID the client polls.

Celery is the long-established Python task queue: app = Celery("worker", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0"), @app.task on a function, build_report.delay(owner_id) to enqueue it, and celery -A worker worker --loglevel=INFO to run the workers.
Queues add retries with back-off, scheduled jobs (Celery beat), stored results and scaling by adding workers; lighter alternatives include RQ, Dramatiq and ARQ.
Make tasks idempotent and pass IDs, not objects: a retried task must not charge a card twice, and the worker should load fresh data from the database.
Keep job state where every process can see it: an in-memory dict works for one process only, and is lost on a restart or invisible to other workers.
Use BackgroundTasks for small in-process jobs, and a queue when work is slow, must survive restarts, needs retries or must run on other machines.

lessons.title: TestClient and test structure
objectives: Test endpoints in-process with TestClient
Organise a FastAPI test suite with fixtures in conftest.py
key_points: TestClient, from fastapi.testclient, wraps the app in an HTTPX client that calls it in-process, with no server: client.post("/auth/token", data={...}) returns a response with .status_code, .headers and .json().
Use it as a context manager, with TestClient(app) as client:, so the lifespan's start-up and shutdown run as they would in production.
Share set-up through fixtures in conftest.py: a client, a test database, and a factory such as make_user() that registers a user and returns the Authorization header.
Test behaviour through the HTTP interface, including the failure paths: 401 without a token, 404 for another user's task, 409 for a taken username and 422 for invalid input.
Settings are often read at import time, so set test values, such as a test secret key and database URL, in conftest.py before importing the app.

lessons.title: Overriding dependencies
objectives: Swap dependencies for tests with dependency_overrides
Design dependencies so they're easy to override
key_points: app.dependency_overrides[original] = replacement swaps a dependency for every request in a test; clear the dictionary afterwards so tests can't affect each other.
Design for overriding: when request sessions and background jobs both get their session factory from one dependency, overriding that one moves everything onto the test database.
Override get_settings to give tests their own configuration, such as a temporary outbox file, without touching the environment.
Override outside services, such as payments, email or other APIs, with fakes that record their calls, so tests are fast, repeatable and never touch real systems.
Overrides are keyed by the function object the app uses, so import the same function from the same module.

lessons.title: Isolated test databases and async tests
objectives: Give every test a fresh, isolated database
Write async tests and measure coverage
key_points: Tests must never touch production or shared data: give each test a fresh database, created by a fixture and thrown away afterwards.

In-memory SQLite is fast: create_engine("sqlite://", connect_args={"check_same_thread": False}, poolclass=StaticPool) keeps one connection, so every session in the test sees the same database; create the tables with Base.metadata.create_all(engine).
SQLite isn't PostgreSQL: types, constraints and concurrency differ, so also run the suite against the production engine, such as PostgreSQL in a container or a CI service container, before deploying.

For tests that must await other async code, use httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test") in a test marked @pytest.mark.anyio; the anyio pytest plugin comes with AnyIO, which FastAPI depends on.
Measure coverage with pytest --cov and keep the reports in CI: a suite you trust is what makes frequent deployment safe.

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://test") as client:
        response = await client.get("/health")
    assert response.json() == {"status": "ok"}

modules.title: Production Deployment
modules.summary: Run the service for real: configuration and secrets from the environment, a Docker image built for production, workers, performance and structured logs, and deployment behind an Nginx reverse proxy with health checks.

lessons.title: Configuration and secrets
objectives: Configure a FastAPI service from environment variables with pydantic-settings
Keep secrets out of code, images and logs
key_points: Configuration that differs between environments, such as the database URL, secret key, log level and allowed origins, comes from environment variables, not code, so one image runs anywhere.

pydantic-settings: a Settings(BaseSettings) class with model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="TASKHUB_", env_file=".env") reads TASKHUB_DATABASE_URL and the rest, converts and validates them, and stops at start-up when a required one is missing.

Declare secrets as SecretStr: the value is hidden in reprs and logs and read deliberately with get_secret_value(). Give the secret key no default, so a forgotten setting stops the app instead of running with a known key.
Read the settings once, with @lru_cache on get_settings(), and inject them with Depends(get_settings) where they're needed, so tests can override them.

.env files are for development: keep them out of Git and out of images (.gitignore and .dockerignore), and supply real secrets through the platform, such as Docker or Kubernetes secrets or a secrets manager.

lessons.title: Docker images for FastAPI
objectives: Write a production Dockerfile for a FastAPI service
Run it with health checks and the right network settings
key_points: Start from an official slim Python image, copy requirements.txt and install it before copying the code, so Docker reuses the cached dependency layer whenever only the code changes.

Use the exec form of CMD, such as CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"] or CMD ["fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "8000"], so the server is PID 1, gets the stop signal and shuts down cleanly, lifespan included.
Run as an unprivileged user (useradd, then USER appuser), and list in .dockerignore what must stay out of the image: .venv, .git, tests, .env and local databases.
Inside a container the server must listen on 0.0.0.0, because 127.0.0.1 there is reachable only from inside the container; docker run -p 8000:8000 publishes the port.

A HEALTHCHECK, or the orchestrator's own probe, calls an endpoint such as /health, and Docker Compose's depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for it before starting the services that need the app.
Pin the base image and dependency versions for repeatable builds, and use a multi-stage build when compilers or build tools are needed only to install dependencies.

lessons.title: Workers, performance and logging
objectives: Choose how many processes to run, and how
Find performance problems, and log so that problems can be found
key_points: One Uvicorn process uses one CPU core. Run several with uvicorn --workers 4 or fastapi run --workers 4, or with Gunicorn as the process manager: gunicorn app.main:app -k uvicorn_worker.UvicornWorker -w 4, from the uvicorn-worker package (the older uvicorn.workers module is deprecated).
Under Kubernetes or another orchestrator, run one process per container and scale by adding containers; use workers when you manage a server or virtual machine yourself.
Workers are separate processes with their own memory: in-memory caches, rate limits and job stores aren't shared, so keep shared state in the database or Redis.

Performance basics: don't block the event loop, reuse database and HTTP connection pools, paginate long lists, declare response models (recent FastAPI serialises them with Pydantic's Rust core), and measure with a load-testing tool such as Locust before tuning.

Log to standard error, one JSON object per line, with a request ID passed back in X-Request-ID and the method, path, status and duration of every request; never log tokens, passwords or Authorization headers.

lessons.title: Behind a reverse proxy, with health checks
objectives: Serve the app behind Nginx with the forwarded headers it needs
Separate liveness from readiness
key_points: A reverse proxy such as Nginx or Traefik sits in front of the app server: it terminates HTTPS, buffers slow clients, balances load across instances and can serve static files, while the app listens only on a private network.

Nginx passes requests on with proxy_pass http://app:8000; and proxy_set_header lines for Host, X-Forwarded-For ($proxy_add_x_forwarded_for) and X-Forwarded-Proto ($scheme), so the app learns the client's address and the original scheme.
Uvicorn uses the forwarded headers only from addresses in --forwarded-allow-ips, which defaults to 127.0.0.1: set it to the proxy's address, or to * only when nothing but the proxy can reach the app.

If the proxy serves the API under a prefix such as /api and strips it, start the server with --root-path /api so the docs and generated URLs include it; the root_path argument of FastAPI() is deprecated in recent versions.
Expose a liveness check (/health: the process answers) and a readiness check (/ready: the database answers too), so proxies, Docker and orchestrators send traffic only to instances that can serve it.

import json
import logging
import time
import uuid
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from sqlalchemy import text

from app import auth, tasks
from app.config import get_settings
from app.database import SessionDep

log = logging.getLogger("app")


class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    """One JSON object per line: easy for log collectors to parse and search."""

    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        entry = {"time": self.formatTime(record, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"), "level": record.levelname,
                 "logger": record.name, "message": record.getMessage()}
        entry.update(getattr(record, "fields", {}))
        return json.dumps(entry)


def setup_logging(level: str, as_json: bool) -> None:
    handler = logging.StreamHandler()  # standard error: Docker and systemd collect it
    plain = logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")
    handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter() if as_json else plain)
    logging.basicConfig(level=level, handlers=[handler], force=True)


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    settings = get_settings()
    setup_logging(settings.log_level, settings.log_json)
    settings.outbox_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    log.info("TaskHub starting")
    yield
    log.info("TaskHub stopping")


app = FastAPI(title="TaskHub", version="1.0.0", lifespan=lifespan)
app.include_router(auth.router)
app.include_router(tasks.router)
app.include_router(tasks.reports)


@app.middleware("http")
async def log_requests(request: Request, call_next):
    """Give every request an ID, pass it back in X-Request-ID, and log one line per request."""
    request_id = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID") or uuid.uuid4().hex[:16]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    duration_ms = round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000, 1)
    response.headers["X-Request-ID"] = request_id
    # TODO 1: log one INFO line, "request", with extra={"fields": {...}} holding request_id, the
    #        method, the path, the status code, duration_ms and the client's address (request.client.host)
    return response


@app.get("/health", tags=["service"])
def health() -> dict[str, str]:
    """Liveness: the process is up and answering."""
    return {"status": "ok"}


@app.get("/ready", tags=["service"])
def ready(session: SessionDep) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Readiness: the database answers too, so this instance can take traffic."""
    # TODO 2: run SELECT 1 with session.execute(text("SELECT 1")); if it raises an exception,
    #        log it and raise a 503 with the detail "Database unavailable"; otherwise return {"status": "ready"}
    return {"status": "ready"}

FROM python:3.13-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

WORKDIR /code

# Dependencies first: this layer is rebuilt only when requirements.txt changes.
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY alembic.ini .
COPY migrations ./migrations
COPY app ./app

# Run as an unprivileged user, with a folder for the SQLite file and the outbox.
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser && mkdir /data && chown appuser /data
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s \
    CMD ["python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/health', timeout=2)"]

# Exec form, so uvicorn is PID 1 and receives the stop signal. Behind a proxy, trust its headers.
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--proxy-headers", "--forwarded-allow-ips", "*"]

.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
*.db
outbox.jsonl
tests/
.pytest_cache/
htmlcov/
.git/

services:
  app:
    build: .
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      TASKHUB_DATABASE_URL: sqlite:////data/taskhub.db
      TASKHUB_OUTBOX_PATH: /data/outbox.jsonl
      TASKHUB_LOG_JSON: "true"
    # Migrate, then replace the shell with uvicorn so it receives stop signals.
    command: ["sh", "-c", "alembic upgrade head && exec uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips '*'"]
    volumes:
      - taskhub-data:/data
    expose:
      - "8000"
    restart: unless-stopped

  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      app:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  taskhub-data:

# Copy to .env and put a real secret in it: python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))"
TASKHUB_SECRET_KEY=replace-me
TASKHUB_LOG_LEVEL=INFO

hints: If the app container keeps restarting, docker compose logs app shows why; a missing TASKHUB_SECRET_KEY stops it at start-up, by design.
--forwarded-allow-ips '*' is safe here only because the app's port is exposed to the Compose network, not published to the host.
The image runs as appuser, so anything it writes must go in /data, the volume.
Docker Compose v2 is the docker compose command (with a space).

project.title: Ship a secure, containerised task API
project.brief: Take the task management API you built in Introduction to FastAPI and Modern Web Services, or TaskHub from this course, to production quality. Add accounts with the OAuth2 password flow, Argon2-hashed passwords and short-lived JWT access tokens; every user sees only their own projects and tasks, and an admin role can list users. Store everything with SQLAlchemy 2.0, with Alembic migrations that build the schema from an empty database: SQLite by default, and PostgreSQL when the database URL points to it (as an optional third Compose service). Keep report jobs in the database, so they survive restarts and work with several workers, and send notifications with background tasks. Test it thoroughly against an isolated database with dependency overrides. Configure it entirely from environment variables, log JSON lines with request IDs, expose /health and /ready, package it in a Docker image that runs as a non-root user, and serve it with Uvicorn or Gunicorn workers behind Nginx with Docker Compose. Optionally, deploy the same image to a Linux server or a cloud platform of your choice, with HTTPS.
deliverables: The code or a repository link: the app package, migrations, tests, Dockerfile, .dockerignore, compose.yaml and nginx.conf
At least 25 tests with at least 85% coverage, isolated from any real database
Alembic migrations that build the schema from an empty database, including one safe change: a new column with a server default
A README covering every environment variable, running locally, running with Docker Compose, and the API's security model
A transcript through the proxy: register, log in, create and list tasks, a 401, a 404 for another user's task, a report job polled until done, and docker compose ps with the app healthy
Optional: the URL of a server or cloud deployment, and how HTTPS is provided there
